Dusan Zivkovic said that in May and June, EPS recorded the lowest production for those months since ‌the ​Djerdap 1 power plant was opened ⁠in 1970. The plant, ⁠jointly operated by Serbia and Romania, has total installed active power of 1,140 MW. “At the moment, the power plant produces about 5,000 MWh per day, which ​is a third of the average daily production,” Zivkovic told Reuters. Energy Minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said on Wednesday ⁠that Serbia’s fuel imports fell ⁠to 25% of their monthly target for ​July as low Danube water levels in Hungary, Serbia and ​Romania forced barges and tankers to operate at ‌30% to 40% of their cargo capacity. The low levels of the Danube have impacted other Serbian energy facilities such as the coal-fired Kostolac power plants, where a lack ⁠of water affected cooling systems, leading to lower output, Zivkovic said. He warned of more problems ahead, but pledged a stable ⁠supply of electricity ‌to the nation of around 6.5 ⁠million. “Unfortunately, forecasts are not any better, and ​some ‌suggest that at the beginning of August ​we will ⁠have (Danube water) inflows of about 1,500 cubic meters per second, which is the biological minimum,” he said. Serbia’s hydrometeorological department forecast a minimal rise in the Danube in the coming days due to rainfall upstream. https://bnn-news.com/latvian-ports-are-n.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home Baltics Latvia Latvia Money Latvian ports are not refusing to accept domestic grain BNN September 8, 2026 Facebook Twitter Photo: Kaspars Nordens/LETA The Ministry of Transport has no information about Latvian ports refusing to accept domestic grain, the ministry told BNN. Companies providing transportation services strictly comply with all applicable sanctions, while the competent authorities carry out rigorous controls and supervision throughout the logistics chain. At the same time, handling and storage capacity is sufficient to accommodate all declared domestic grain shipments, according to the information report On Solutions in the Area of Grain Transit, which was reviewed at an extraordinary government meeting on Friday, the 4th of September. The government also decided that ports and state-owned Latvijas dzelzceļš must ensure priority access for the transportation of products from Latvian farmers. Asked how soon laboratory testing to determine the origin of grain would begin, the Ministry of Transport said the government had decided at the meeting to grant the Food and Veterinary Service (PVD) the right to inspect grain cargo in transit at Latvian ports, including verifying its origin. At the same time, the ministry noted that this issue does not fall within its area of responsibility. In an interview with Latvijas Radio, PVD Director General Māris Balodis said the service currently does not inspect transit cargo. However, if the government amends the Cabinet regulations governing border controls, the PVD will be authorised to inspect the documentation accompanying such cargo and take grain samples to analyse their possible geographical origin. Balodis also said that several foreign laboratories would have to be involved in determining the geographical origin of grain transported in transit, stressing that the procedure is not inexpensive. The PVD Director General added that it would be a paid service, with the cost covered by the cargo sender. The analyses would take approximately one month, while testing a single shipment could cost an estimated 900,000 euros. Balodis explained that the PVD would take a grain sample after receiving advance payment. If the cargo sender refuses to pay, the shipment would not be allowed to cross Latvia’s border. The government is expected to take a specific decision on granting these powers in mid-September. Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Delcy Rodríguez and Donald Trump pose for a picture together on Tuesday. Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty Images Delcy Rodríguez Delcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearby Venezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessor Tom Phillips Latin America correspondent Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.54 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez , has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president, less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro. The former foes met at a five-star hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower in Manhattan late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas in January. From socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez Read more On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply. But she did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of Venezuela’s diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly. “We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally. Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera. A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. “It was a short meeting but it was an important meeting,” Rubio said on Wednesday, telling reporters it had focused on Venezuela’s economic recovery and political transition. Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as Rodríguez appeared to wince. View image in fullscreen Observers suggested Delcy Rodríguez’s clenched left hand signified her discomfort around Donald Trump. Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty Images Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appeared to be clenching her left fist. Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against American imperialism. After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”. One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez-Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer” . But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy. Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week but failed. ​Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, rejected the idea that Rodríguez had been humiliated by her meeting with Trump. “It’s a huge triumph [for her]. She got the photo op she wanted. I frankly don’t think you can overestimate how important the photo op was for her,” said Pérez, who believed the image legitimised Rodríguez’s position as president and signalled that Washington was happy to keep working with her and for other leaders to engage with her. For Trump, meeting Rodríguez was a way to show Maga voters he had “won Venezuela” by commandeering its massive oil reserves with January’s invasion. “So that picture was a win-win for Delcy and for Trump ,” Pérez added. Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions. At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard. As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure. Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote. “Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/drone-fr.text: Drone fragments found on romanian beach. The military neutralized them The Ministry of National Defense (MApN) announced that on Thursday morning an EOD team from the Romanian Naval Forces traveled to the Capu Midia beach area to check for debris from an aerial drone. Following verification, it was determined that the fragments did not have an explosive charge. They were neutralized on site, around 9.30 am. The drone debris was reported in the beach area on Wednesday evening, around 8:00 p.m. „Due to darkness falling, it was decided to isolate the area, with the intervention being postponed until this morning,” the Ministry of National Defense announced. Drone fragments found on several beaches This is not the first case of its kind this year. In recent months, fragments presumed to be from drones have been found on the beaches of Eforie Nord , Olimp, Costinești and Constanța.
